title: Critical Kasner scaling from Cauchy-horizon collapse near holographic phase transitions
authors: Ling-Long Gao, Yan Liu, Hong-Da Lyu
abstract: We study continuous scalar-hair bifurcations from stationary black holes with a nonextremal Cauchy horizon. Although the exterior deformation vanishes at criticality, the critical zero mode generically develops a logarithmic branch at the reference Cauchy horizon, producing a nonuniform critical limit. We show that the coefficient of this logarithm in the scalar perturbation, together with local Cauchy-horizon data, determines the exponential collapse rate of the Einstein-Rosen bridge. If the post-collapse geometry evolves into a Kasner regime, the boundary order-parameter scaling $O\propto|λ-λ_c|^β$ further implies $   1-p_t\propto|λ-λ_c|^{2β}. $ Crucially, zero-mode matching fixes both the critical exponents and the associated amplitudes, without any fit to the nonlinear interior. We illustrate this mechanism in the transition from rotating BTZ to hairy rotating black holes. For scalarized RN-AdS$_4$ black branes, we quantitatively verify the predicted Kasner scaling using fully nonlinear numerical solutions. At low temperature, two charged models with identical linear critical data instead approach different infrared endpoints, yielding respectively power-law and inverse-logarithmic Kasner scaling. Thus interiors near a finite-temperature bifurcation are controlled by zero-mode transmission, whereas low temperature scaling is governed by the nonlinear infrared completion.
summary: This theoretical work investigates how phase transitions occurring at the boundary of black holes dictate the physics deep inside the black hole, specifically across the Cauchy horizon. By analyzing the zero-mode structure, the authors show that the critical data fixes the scaling laws of the subsequent Kasner epoch. This provides a powerful mechanism for connecting external, measurable parameters to the highly non-trivial, strongly coupled physics of black hole interiors.
main_problem: The study aims to determine how critical data from an exterior phase transition can be transmitted across a black hole's Cauchy horizon to control the scaling behavior of the interior geometry.
main_result: The zero-mode data transmitted across the horizon fixes the critical exponents and amplitudes of the subsequent Kasner epoch, requiring no independent fitting to the nonlinear interior.
method: The analysis uses matched boundary-layer techniques to connect linear zero-mode solutions near the Cauchy horizon to fully nonlinear numerical solutions describing the Einstein-Rosen bridge collapse and the subsequent Kasner regime.
model_or_system: The system involves black holes (e.g., BTZ, RN-AdS branes) undergoing continuous scalar-hair bifurcations, where the dynamics are governed by coupled Einstein equations and scalar field equations.
key_observables: Critical exponents ($ eta$), the exponential collapse rate ($\Gamma_{ER}$), and the scaling laws for the Kasner epoch ($1-p_t \propto |\lambda-\lambda_c|^{2 eta}$).
important_parameters: The boundary control parameter $\lambda$, the critical point $\lambda_c$, and the zero-mode coefficient $B^-$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a nonextremal Cauchy horizon and relies on matching linear zero-mode solutions to nonlinear boundary layer physics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the physical process across the black hole interior: from the asymptotic AdS boundary, through the Cauchy horizon, across the ER collapse, and into the final Kasner epoch.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the linear zero-mode behavior near the Cauchy horizon, then developing the nonlinear matching procedure across the ER bridge, and finally applying this framework to derive the scaling laws in the subsequent Kasner epoch, contrasting low-temperature vs. near-bifurcation physics.
why_interesting: The concept of transmitting boundary conditions (like critical exponents) from an external, well-defined phase transition (the bifurcation) into the deep, strongly coupled, and singular interior of a black hole provides an analogy for how external perturbations dictate the low-energy physics of complex quantum systems.
